articles.title: Towards a Reciprocal Datafication Model: How data flows in our digitally mediated reality
articles.authors: Chiara A E Wüller, Alex van der Zeeuw, Maximilian A Friehs, Alexander J A M van Deursen
articles.abstract: This contribution explores the deep entanglement of datafication in our digitally mediated reality and introduces the Reciprocal Datafication Model (RDM) as a conceptual framework for understanding how individuals shape and are shaped by data. While data offers opportunities for optimization and participation, it simultaneously reinforces inequalities and power asymmetries, manifesting in phenomena such as surveillance capitalism and data colonialism. Centering the individual, RDM conceptualizes datafication as a reciprocal process across three interrelated flows: the structural flow, which captures socio-technical infrastructures and power relations, the critical flow in which data practices are socially negotiated and oriented towards optimization or surveillance, and the self-relevance flow, where data shapes meaning-making and cognitive processing. RDM bridges individual data practices and broader social structures, while contributing to communication theory by offering an analytically grounded approach to understanding how digitally mediated realities are produced, experienced, and governed, and how individuals navigate emerging inequalities within them.

articles.title: Archives of power: Algorithmic memory, ideological (Re)production and negotiation of hegemonic masculinity
articles.authors: Silas Udenze
articles.abstract: This article examines how algorithmic memory shapes the production and negotiation of masculinity in the context of Nigeria. Inductively adopting Connell’s theory of hegemonic masculinity as an interpretive framework, the article attempts to understand how digital platforms mediate men’s self-perceptions amid economic precarities and shifting gender expectations. The analysis of two focus group discussions with men aged 24 to 45, the author constructed three interrelated dynamics: Algorithmic temporal dislocation (How resurfaced memories evoke shame and anxiety over economic failure); Memory curation as counter-memory (Strategies to reassert agency over algorithmic authorship and dominance); and Platformed provision and performing masculinity (Online visibility as a performative substitute for material provision), which explain how algorithmic systems shape and reproduce ideals of hegemonic masculinity. By locating algorithmic memory within the cultural politics of masculinity in Africa, this article advances our understanding of digital media as spaces where algorithms shape whose memories are amplified, whose identities are recognized, and how existing gender and social inequalities are reproduced and contested.

articles.title: Fan translation as memetic communication: Understanding cultural diffusion through cross-cultural fan labour
articles.authors: Seryun Lee
articles.abstract: This article explores the role of online fan translation in the cross-cultural consumption and dissemination of popular culture through a case study of the production and reproduction of translated K-pop content across different genres and platforms. It proposes memetic communication as a conceptual framework for understanding cultural diffusion through fan translation. While internet memes are recognised as a ubiquitous digital media practice, this study attempts to theorise memetic communication as a vital mode of online communication that penetrates various kinds of content reproduction and audience engagement in popular culture, with a focus on fan translation. More specifically, this article illustrates how memetic communication – that is, cultural reproduction driven by creative imitation and manipulation – is akin to fan translation, which often involves innovative remediation practices and grassroots distribution. It also investigates how translation can be an integral part of broader memetic communication by establishing textual relationships with other content, including that which is fan-produced. This study’s key argument is that translation permeates the different processes of content production and dissemination, thereby facilitating cultural diffusion.

articles.title: From Algorithms to Affection: Unpacking the Psychological Mechanism of Emotional Attachment Toward Virtual Influencers
articles.authors: Hyun Jung Oh, Mikyoung Kim
articles.abstract: As virtual human influencers (VHIs) increasingly inhabit social media landscapes, they are functioning not merely as marketing tools but as social entities capable of eliciting user affection. However, the psychological mechanisms underlying emotional attachment to these artificial agents remain underexplored compared to their human counterparts. This study investigates how VHI self-disclosure influences emotional attachment, positing parasocial relationships as a mediator and perceived attractiveness and humanness as boundary conditions. We analyzed online survey data from 540 young adults familiar with VHIs using a moderated mediation framework. The findings reveal a complex dynamic distinct from human interaction: VHI self-disclosure generally hindered parasocial relationship formation unless the VHI was perceived as physically attractive. This suggests attractiveness acts as a requisite gateway for users to accept artificial disclosure as relationally meaningful. Subsequently, parasocial relationships strongly predicted emotional attachment, an effect significantly amplified by perceived humanness. Consequently, self-disclosure indirectly promoted emotional attachment only when the VHI was viewed as both attractive and human-like. These results delineate the distinct roles of VHI attributes: Attractiveness facilitates the initial establishment of a social connection (parasocial relationship), whereas perceived humanness deepens this bond into a meaningful emotional attachment. Theoretically, this study expands the understanding of human–agent interaction by identifying these differential pathways. Practically, it suggests that developers must prioritize high visual attractiveness to make VHI interactions acceptable, while simultaneously imbuing agents with human-like qualities to foster lasting emotional loyalty.

articles.title: Historical Grand Strategy as Selective Causal Modeling: Civil–Military Coupling, Causal Legibility, and the Limits of Playable History
articles.authors: Yuancheng Si
articles.abstract: Historical grand strategy games cannot model every aspect of the past. They must decide which relationships to represent in detail and which to simplify. This article examines the consequences of those choices through Hearts of Iron IV (with version 1.19.2), focusing on the limited connections between its civilian economy and military systems. A close analysis of the game's mechanics, compared with scholarship on wartime mobilization, shows a clear asymmetry: military production is represented in considerable detail, while the civilian economy is compressed into a much smaller set of aggregate variables. This matters not simply because the game is an imperfect representation of history. It shapes the kind of history that becomes visible in play. Wartime mobilization is presented primarily as the conversion of civilian resources into military power, while many of the social costs, institutional constraints, and feedback effects of that conversion remain less visible. In turn, these design choices influence which counterfactual questions players can readily explore and, particularly for players with limited prior knowledge, might influence their expectations about how wartime economies worked. The article concludes by considering the broader trade offs faced by historical simulations between causal adequacy, cognitive tractability, strategic choices, and commercial accessibility, with ethical representation treated as a further constraint.

articles.title: Beyond Fairy Tales: Post-Fairy-Tale Narrative Identity and Therapeutic Ambiguity in FromSoftware's Souls Games
articles.authors: Tibor Guzsvinecz, Bendegúz Lajos Kovács, Judit Szűcs, Peter Zoltan Kada, Renata Cserjesi
articles.abstract: Scholarship on FromSoftware's Souls games has read them largely as tests of skill, leaving open how they function as meaning-making narrative systems. This article introduces the post-fairy-tale narrative system as an analytic category: a structure that retains the symbolic apparatus of the fairy tale while withdrawing its guarantee structure, the assurance of moral clarity, closure, and restoration that folklore scholarship treats as the consoling core of the classic Western form. Its conceptual contribution is therapeutic ambiguity, a mode in which confrontation with fear, loss, and uncertainty is sustained without containment, so that meaning shifts from narrative outcome to endurance, repetition, and embodied learning. Examining titles from Demon's Souls (2009) to Elden Ring: Nightreign (2025) as Japanese works rather than against a universal Western template, the article offers a culturally situated, narratologically grounded framework for game studies.

articles.title: The programmed organization decentralized autonomous organizations and the transformation of organizational decision architectures
articles.authors: Jonathan Harth, Georgios Alexiou
articles.abstract: Purpose This article examines decentralized autonomous organizations (DAOs) through Luhmann's systems theory, asking what happens when organizational decision premises are no longer communicatively constituted and interpreted but compiled and executed as code. The concept of the “programmed organization” captures the decisive shift: a displacement of organizational contingency from operation to governance. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Luhmann's organization theory and recent systems-theoretical work on digital transformation, we conduct a conceptual, ideal-typical analysis guided by the distinction programme/code and centered on a definition of governance as the deciding of decision premises. Three reference cases varying in function and governance design (Sky/MakerDAO, Uniswap, MolochDAO) discipline the reconstruction of all four premise dimensions: programmes, personnel, communication channels and organizational culture. Findings DAOs instantiate a “hybrid autopoiesis”: self-reproduction that remains communicative while structurally coupled to the machine production of decision events. Smart-contract execution does not communicate; it is communicated – attributed as decisions of the organization. Smart contracts thereby heighten the technization of conditional programmes: a difference of degree, not a categorical break. What distinguishes DAOs is not any single element but the configuration: the fixing of contingency is delegated to machine execution while its renewed opening concentrates in governance – operations are computed rather than decided, and the undecidable questions gather where premises are written, audited and revised. Trust is thus not eliminated but displaced: from persons to code, from operation to governance. DAOs represent organizational evolution rather than revolution. Originality/value Beyond a systematic application of Luhmann's programme concept to DAOs – bridging the technical and sociological meanings of “programme” – the “programmed organization” names a mechanism rather than another label: it specifies where automation can take hold within the architecture of decision premises and where the contingency thus removed reappears, thereby illuminating the programmatic architectures of digital society.

articles.title: What factors build user trust in human–technology relationships? An exploratory meta-analysis of the key antecedents to trust in IT artifacts
articles.authors: Thuy Duong Oesterreich, Eduard Anton, Matthias Söllner, Frank Teuteberg
articles.abstract: Purpose In response to various calls for more research extending our understanding of trust in IT artifacts, we synthesize the empirical evidence of prior studies in the rich stream of trust-related research to gain a more consistent picture regarding the role of trust antecedents in human–technology relationships. Design/methodology/approach We conduct an exploratory meta-analysis of 374 primary studies reported in 348 articles covering 26 years of trust research to gain deeper insights into the role of the antecedents to trust in IT artifacts. Our research framework combines 19 independent variables conceptualizing human- and system-like trusting beliefs, technology acceptance factors, system characteristics, user characteristics and contextual factors with perceived risk, trusting intention and trusting behavior as the dependent variables. Findings The findings confirm the pervasive role of the human- and system-like trusting beliefs ability/competence, benevolence, reliability and helpfulness as well as the technology acceptance factors perceived enjoyment and perceived usefulness in building trust and fostering trusting behavior. In addition, the findings indicate the importance of the system characteristics security and privacy in forming trust and helping users overcome the perceived degree of uncertainty on the way to fostering behavioral and continuous intention. Originality/value Based on the findings, we discuss the implications for research and practice, propose design recommendations for increasing trust in IT artifacts and provide future research avenues to explore. Considering that trust significantly influences IT adoption, our study's integrated perspective on trust is crucial for deepening our understanding of key factors in fostering trust between humans and technology.

articles.title: How AI agents’ self-disclosure in initial interactions shapes user perceptions: evidence from dual cognitive pathways
articles.authors: Minqian Yang, Pei-Luen Patrick Rau
articles.abstract: Purpose As users increasingly engage with various unfamiliar artificial intelligence (AI) agents, initial impressions become crucial. AI agents’ self-disclosure can play a key role in shaping these impressions. This study aims to conceptualize AI agents’ self-disclosure, identify key user perceptual factors and examine how self-disclosure influences user perceptions through different cognitive pathways. Design/methodology/approach A two-stage questionnaire survey was conducted. Firstly, exploratory factor analysis was employed to identify key perceptual factors shaped by AI self-disclosure and to examine their effects on users’ willingness to use. Then, users’ willingness to use the AI agents adopting different self-disclosure styles across utilitarian and hedonic scenarios was investigated, and the underlying cognitive mechanisms were further analyzed. Findings Three core perceptual factors were identified: perceived social individuality, perceived reliability and perceived emotional support. In both utilitarian and hedonic scenarios, users consistently preferred an emotional (over factual) tone for relation-oriented self-disclosure, which incorporated richer social cues, and a detailed (over brief) style for transparency-oriented self-disclosure, which conveyed more machine-related characteristics. Perceived social individuality was found to play a more important role in users’ evaluation of AI agents’ relation-oriented self-disclosure. The results provide empirical support for a dual perspective of AI agents that can be shaped by self-disclosure: relation-oriented self-disclosure activates social responses, whereas transparency-oriented self-disclosure triggers machine-based evaluations. Originality/value This study proposes and empirically validates the concept of AI self-disclosure as a dual-dimensional construct. By uncovering the mechanisms through which it shapes initial perceptions, it offers actionable insights for designing more transparent and socially attuned AI agents.

articles.title: Anticipatory resilience in complex systems: a Luhmannian-cybernetic framework for critical infrastructure
articles.authors: Sergio Jofre, Giedre Sabaliauskaite
articles.abstract: Purpose This article reconceptualises anticipatory resilience (AR) in complex sociotechnical organisational environment, notably critical infrastructure (CI) organisations by integrating Luhmann’s social systems theory and cybernetic principles. It addresses the limitations of control-oriented AR frameworks by proposing a communicative understanding centred on programmes, decision premises and second-order observation. Design/methodology/approach The article introduces a framework positioning organisations as autopoietic decision systems that maintain resilience through recursive communication and adaptive programmatic coordination. AR is operationalised via organisational programmes, structural couplings, distributed variety and reflexive observation, illustrated through an emergency medical services (EMS) worked example facing cyber and hybrid threats. Findings The study finds that AR emerges not from predictive accuracy or centralised control but from an organisation’s capacity to recursively stabilise and revise future-oriented expectations under uncertainty. Programmes operate as executable communication architectures that organise attention, operationalise inclusion/exclusion and coordinate heterogeneous digital and analogue environments. Originality/value The article reframes anticipation as a communicative accomplishment grounded in organisational decision-making rather than forecasting. It advances debates on digital governance by conceptualising programmes as sociotechnical architectures shaping operational relevance, communicative inclusion and adaptive governance within programmable CI organisations.

articles.title: Assimilating generative AI into ideation work: seeding, search and human contribution
articles.authors: Jafar Sabbah, Aneesh Banerjee, Feng Li
articles.abstract: Purpose This paper examines how generative AI (GenAI) systems can be assimilated into idea generation (ideation) work so that human–GenAI collaboration augments creativity. It asks which seeding configurations with GenAI improve novelty, utility and feasibility, and examines preliminary process evidence regarding human contribution to joint search. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on a search-based view of creativity, we conceptualise GenAI as an information system that structures individuals' search and evaluation of information. We test four configurations with 400 professionals: human-only ideation, unstructured human–GenAI collaboration, GenAI seeding and a TC-based GenAI configuration. Expert evaluators rate novelty, utility and feasibility. Findings Statistically reliable improvements in novelty, utility, or feasibility were not detected for either unstructured human–GenAI collaboration or conventional GenAI seeding. The TC-based GenAI configuration, by contrast, significantly improves novelty relative to unstructured collaboration and conventional seeding. Statistically significant differences in utility were not detected relative to either GenAI comparison condition, while feasibility was lower relative to conventional seeding. Practical implications Organisations should not assume that simply enabling GenAI in ideation tools will improve creative outcomes. When seeking to promote novelty, organisations may consider the full TC-based GenAI configuration tested here, combining a short TC orientation with TC-based GenAI-generated seeds. Originality/value The study advances information systems research on AI assimilation and human–AI collaboration by showing that creative augmentation is not automatic and depends on how GenAI is configured to structure joint search. It identifies the TC-based GenAI configuration as a concrete way to enhance novelty in human–GenAI ideation.

articles.title: Antecedents and consequences of face filter use on social media: the role of use frequency and depth
articles.authors: Jingjing Tong, Chunyi Xian, Jingjun (David) Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose Face filters are pervasive in selfie-based social media practices, raising concerns about their psychological implications. This study examines the social drivers of face-filter use frequency and depth, their positive and negative psychological consequences and how these two dimensions jointly shape user outcomes. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on self-discrepancy theory (SDT), we conceptualize descriptive and subjective norms as self-guides influencing two dimensions of filter use: frequency (which regulates discrepancy accessibility) and depth (which regulates discrepancy availability). We propose a model linking filter use to affective outcomes and self-evaluations and examine the interactive effects of use frequency and depth on these outcomes. The model was tested using survey data from 328 participants. Findings Descriptive and subjective norms positively predict use frequency and depth. Use frequency, but not use depth, increases self-confidence by enhancing appearance self-esteem; whereas both frequency and depth increase negative moods by amplifying self-discrepancy perceptions. Additionally, the interaction between use frequency and depth is positively associated with both appearance self-esteem and perceived self-discrepancy. Originality/value This study is among the first to integrate SDT and social norms to explain the antecedents and dual consequences of face-filter use. By distinguishing use frequency and depth as two self-regulation dimensions in digital self-presentation, this study highlights their main and interactive effects on positive and negative psychological outcomes and clarifies the underlying mechanisms.

articles.title: When AI summarizes the community: how generative AI summaries shape users’ intention to engage with original content
articles.authors: Qian Liu, Shuang Wu, Lin Xu
articles.abstract: Purpose The integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) into user-generated content (UGC) communities has fundamentally reshaped how users seek and consume information. Many UGC platforms, such as RedNote and Zhihu, now incorporate GenAI summaries that provide concise, AI-generated answers at the top of search results. While these summaries improve efficiency, they may also reduce user attention to original community posts, thereby threatening engagement and participation within UGC ecosystems. This study aims to examine how GenAI summary design influences users’ intention to engage with community content and the underlying psychological mechanisms. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on Socio-Technical Systems Theory (STS), this research develops a socio-cognitive model linking AI summary design (source localness and source transparency) to engagement intentions through collective psychological ownership and interest-type curiosity. Two online experiments were conducted: Experiment 1 tested the main and mediating effects, and Experiment 2 introduced query type (subjective-experiential vs objective-analytic) as a contextual moderator. Findings Results reveal two socio-cognitive pathways linking GenAI summary design to user engagement. Community-focused and aggregate-list summaries enhance engagement via collective ownership, whereas web-wide and item-level citation summaries foster curiosity-driven engagement. These effects are contingent on query type: subjective-experiential queries strengthen the ownership pathway, while objective-analytic queries amplify the curiosity pathway. Originality/value This study extends STS to AI-mediated content ecosystems by conceptualizing GenAI summaries as socio-technical interfaces. It advances our understanding of how interface-level design transforms technological affordances into social and cognitive motivations that sustain participation in digital communities.

articles.title: Perks or perils? The dual effect of artificial intelligence-augmented human resource management digitization on employee performance
articles.authors: Ahsan Ali, Waseem Bahadur, Lu Liu, Hussain Tariq
articles.abstract: Purpose This study aims to examine why artificial intelligence-augmented human resource management (AI-HRM) digitization has mixed implications for employee performance. By drawing on person–environment fit theory and sensemaking theory, we propose a contingent dual-pathway model in which AI-HRM digitization affects employee performance through job-related cynicism and innovative job behavior, with task discretion shaping the pathways. Design/methodology/approach We tested the hypotheses by using three-wave time-lagged multisource survey data from full-time employees and their direct supervisors in China (N = 543 employee–supervisor dyads). Findings AI-HRM digitization has no significant direct relationship with employee performance when the mediating mechanisms are considered. Instead, the construct functions through two opposing indirect pathways, that is, a negative pathway through job-related cynicism and a positive pathway through innovative job behavior, with task discretion moderating both pathways. Specifically, high task discretion can weaken the cynicism-based pathway but strengthen the innovation-based pathway, whereas low task discretion can strengthen the cynicism-based pathway but weaken the innovation-based pathway or make it nonsignificant. Originality/value Our study advances a contingent dual-pathway model of AI-HRM digitization by showing that the same digital HR transformation mechanism can elicit defensive and proactive employee responses simultaneously. By identifying task discretion as a key boundary condition, the study can explain when AI-HRM digitization will undermine or enhance employee performance and thus moves beyond simple net-effect explanations for AI-HRM outcomes.

articles.title: Promotion or substitution? The effect of AI assistants on physician performance in online healthcare platforms
articles.authors: Weicheng Wang, Shaoqi Zhang, Min Zhang, Xitong Guo
articles.abstract: Purpose Artificial intelligence (AI) is fundamentally reshaping healthcare delivery. Physician-specific AI assistants, trained on individual physicians’ medical data, now provide personalized medical advice on online healthcare platforms. While AI assistants improve the availability of physician expertise, they may substitute for cognitive tasks traditionally undertaken by physicians. Despite this tension, few studies have examined how AI assistants affect physician performance. This study aims to examine the causal impact of introducing AI assistants on physician consultation volume and how physicians’ existing resource configurations shape this impact. Design/methodology/approach This study leveraged the introduction of AI assistants on a leading online healthcare platform to establish a quasi-natural experimental setting. We constructed a panel dataset covering 3,668 physicians and employed a difference-in-differences model to identify the causal effect of AI assistants on physician performance. Findings The results suggest that the introduction of AI assistants significantly improves physician performance, with physicians experiencing a 3.6% increase in consultation volume. Moderation analyses reveal that the positive effect is weaker for high-reputation physicians and those with broader knowledge. Further heterogeneity analysis shows that the effect is invariant to physician gender but more pronounced among physicians in non-first-tier cities. Originality/value This study provides causal evidence of the impact of AI assistants on individual performance in an online healthcare setting. It further reveals how physicians’ existing resource configurations shape AI’s impact from a resource-based view and offers suggestive evidence on its promotion and substitution pathways.

articles.title: The impact of algorithmic control on app-workers’ counterproductive work behavior: from an objectification perspective
articles.authors: Ming Chi, Yanli Chen, Yongshun Xu, Yuetong Wu, Yihao Yang
articles.abstract: Purpose Drawing on the stressor-strain-outcome model and an objectification perspective, this study examines how algorithmic control is associated with app-workers’ counterproductive work behavior through organizational objectification and self-objectification. It further investigates perceived algorithmic transparency as a boundary condition. Design/methodology/approach Data were collected from 498 DiDi Chuxing drivers in China through a three-wave survey. The measurement model was assessed using SmartPLS 4, while ordinary least squares regression and conditional process analysis in SPSS 27.0 were used to test the direct, indirect, serial mediation, and moderation effects. Findings Algorithmic control was positively associated with counterproductive work behavior through organizational objectification and self-objectification, both separately and sequentially. Perceived algorithmic transparency weakened the positive relationships between algorithmic control and both forms of objectification. Practical implications Algorithmic governance may backfire when workers perceive that they are being treated as instruments or begin to evaluate themselves in instrumental terms. Platforms should reduce instrumental treatment in evaluation and enforcement, provide explanatory feedback, and use targeted transparency to support workers’ understanding of algorithmic decisions. Originality/value This study identifies a sequential objectification mechanism linking algorithmic control to counterproductive work behavior and demonstrates how perceived algorithmic transparency conditions this process.

articles.title: Rejection of cross-cutting news depends on content, sources, and cultural contexts: evidence from online trace data
articles.authors: Wonjeong Jo, Magdalena Wojcieszak
articles.abstract: We examine the conditions in which people reject cross-cutting news in naturalistic settings of online comments. Theoretically, we account for article content and source to test whether commenters’ rejection and its intensity depend on whether cross-cutting news (a) is hostile to their in-group or favorable to the out-group and (b) is “unexpected” (from in-group sources) or “expected” (from out-group sources). Methodologically, we use online traces from news aggregators in South Korea (SK; 7,607 comments) and the United States (116,308 comments). We find that most commenters (79% in SK and 64% in the United States) reject cross-cutting news, with left-leaning commenters expressing stronger rejection than right-leaning commenters. Regarding article content, the SK commenters more strongly rejected in-group hostility, while the U.S. commenters rejected out-group favoritism more. Regarding article source, SK commenters more strongly rejected unexpected cross-cutting news from in-group sources than expected cross-cutting news from out-group sources. We discuss the implications of these findings.

articles.title: Sense of Lack of Control, Cognitive Control, and the Expression of Prejudice: The Role of Effort Withdrawal
articles.authors: Wiktor Soral, Michał Bilewicz
articles.abstract: In contemporary societies, social norms constrain overt prejudice, requiring effortful cognitive processes to monitor and regulate behavior. We propose that diminished personal control is associated with withdrawal of cognitive effort, lower norm-sensitive detection, and greater prejudice expression. Two large-scale nationwide studies (Study 1, N = 1,019; Study 2, N = 1,055) tested this hypothesis. Across both studies, perceived lack of control predicted more frequent overt prejudice, mediated by lower norm-sensitive detection and, in Study 2, also by effort withdrawal. These results suggest that cognitive-regulatory processes may constitute an additional pathway linking perceived lack of control with prejudice expression. More broadly, they highlight the potential role of cognitive resource depletion and norm-sensitive regulation in understanding when prejudiced statements are expressed.

articles.title: The Making of Media Entertainment
articles.authors: Robert Joel Lewis
articles.abstract: Abstract: Entertainment science remains a mosaic of disconnected research streams, each generating valuable insights but lacking a cross-cutting mechanism to reveal their connections. Existing understandings do not link different areas of theory, such as research on entertainment’s appeal versus research on its maladaptive effects. This paper proposes that attending to how entertainment is made can bridge these streams. What entertainment is, on this view, is a technology: entertainment is a deliberately iterated system of superstimuli (unnaturally attention-grabbing stimuli that activate evolved cognitive mechanisms) that producers refine to capture audiences and serve their own goals. Drawing on predictive-mind frameworks from computational neuroscience, this paper treats attention as precision-weighted Bayesian inference and shows how entertainment taps that inference architecture using increasingly sophisticated superstimulus technologies. This view reveals attention capture as a common principle underlying diverse entertainment phenomena. It (a) provides a principled taxonomy that maps research domains onto the evolved mechanisms content activates, (b) reframes and resolves the paradox of suspense, (c) generates first-principles predictions about content evolution and cultivation effects, and (d) helps account for entertainment’s appeal. By identifying what unites disparate research traditions, this approach enables researchers across subfields to position their investigations within a shared theoretical landscape capable of generating cumulative, interconnected knowledge.

articles.title: Deindividuation Among Gendered Violence Survivors and Posting About #MeToo
articles.authors: Shannon Pappas, Kathryn D. Coduto, Jennifer Anderson
articles.abstract: Abstract: Individuals have numerous channels to choose from when posting online, particularly when posting about sensitive or highly personal topics. This study uses the social identity model of deindividuation effects to examine why individuals posted about the #MeToo movement, considering whether they posted about their own experiences as survivors of gendered violence. Specifically, this manuscript offers an alternative theoretical perspective by focusing on positive deindividuation consequences. Participants ( N = 256) completed a survey measuring social identification and perceived anonymity affordances; participants also completed a perceived deindividuation scale that was created for this study and found to be reliable. Results reveal that survivors who posted with #MeToo had stronger group identification with others posting, higher perceptions of anonymity afforded on social network sites, and higher perceptions of deindividuation during #MeToo compared to survivors who chose not to post. This work offers theoretical implications related to positive deindividuating effects, as well as an exploratory measure for deindividuation experiences. Furthermore, this work discusses practical implications related to what makes an online social movement “successful.”

articles.title: Navigating Trans-Parasocial Relationships and Emotional Bonds
articles.authors: Yangna Hu, Cindy S. B. Ngai, Morgan E. Ellithorpe
articles.abstract: Abstract: Social media influencers have emerged as powerful figures in digital culture, engaging followers in relationships that differ from one-sided parasocial dynamics. Scholars have proposed the framework of trans-parasocial relations, characterized by collective reciprocity, synchronous and asynchronous interaction, and co-creation. However, little research has explored this phenomenon among adolescents, who are particularly susceptible to media influence. This study conducted semistructured interviews with 20 Chinese adolescents aged 13–19 to examine their perceived relationships and emotional bonds with influencers. Findings corroborate and extend trans-parasocial relationships in the adolescent context, showing that these connections are imaginably and interactively connected, collectively and selectively reciprocal, and co-created. Importantly, the study reveals a set of distinct emotional bonding patterns in trans-parasocial relationships that diverge from traditional parasocial attachment, characterized by automated proximity, hedonic attachment, familiarity-based security, and flexible commitment. These insights offer a culturally grounded contribution to media psychology and deepen understanding of adolescent engagement in social media environments.

articles.title: Closeness and Well-Being in Older Adulthood: A Dyadic Daily Diary Study
articles.authors: Elizabeth Zambrano Garza, Lynn M. Martire, Yan Huang, Jason Rights, Harry T. Reis
articles.abstract: Relationships are central to well-being. Relationship closeness, which measures interdependence, remains underexplored in older adult couples managing chronic health conditions. In a sample of 146 distinguishable dyads consisting of individuals with chronic back pain (ICBPs) and their spouses, the current study explored the role of own and partner closeness for daily well-being. Additionally, to contextualize ICBPs’ daily experiences, their daily symptoms were assessed as a moderator for these links. Couples completed up to 30 days of end-of-day diaries reporting closeness, affect, and their physical symptoms. Using multilevel models guided by the Actor–Partner Interdependence Model, we found that on days when both ICBPs and spouses reported greater closeness, they experienced higher positive affect and lower negative affect (actor effects). Similarly, partners’ closeness was associated with individuals’ own higher positive and lower negative affect (partner effects) in both ICBPs and spouses. Notably, spouses’ daily affect was more strongly associated with ICBPs’ closeness than their own, suggesting spouses’ heightened susceptibility to ICBPs’ experiences. Contrary to hypotheses, ICBPs’ daily symptoms did not moderate closeness–affect associations for themselves; however, ICBPs’ symptoms moderated partner effects for spouses’ negative affect. Simple slopes analyses revealed that ICBPs’ closeness was beneficial (i.e., decreased negative affect) for spouses across low, average, and high-symptom days; the strength of these associations decreased as symptom levels increased, but remained significant. Findings underscore the importance of dyadic perspectives in understanding well-being in older couples coping with chronic illness.

articles.title: Extra-Familial Intergenerational Contact in the Contemporary United States: Exploring Its Frequency, Nature, and Correlates
articles.authors: Craig Fowler, Jessica Gasiorek
articles.abstract: Some major studies conducted over the last forty years suggest that intergenerational contact between younger and older adults (i.e., those aged 70+) in Western contexts is scarce. However, the phrasing of questions asked in these studies leaves open the possibility that intergenerational contact might not be so rare. In Study 1 ( n = 399), we surveyed young Americans about the frequency and characteristics of their intergenerational interactions. In Study 2 ( n = 278), we surveyed a separate sample of young Americans to assess the quantity and communicative quality of their contact with older people, gather information about their intergenerational relationships, and gauge their attitudes towards aging. In Study 1, 42% of respondents had at least one friend aged 70 or older and over 60% had had contact (typically face-to-face) with an older adult during the previous week. In Study 2, the quality and quantity of contact were associated with the endorsement of prescriptive age-based stereotypes, both directly and indirectly via perceptions of common ingroup identity. Moreover, quantity and quality of contact predicted the affective responses younger adults had at the thought of growing old, and their sense of efficacy about doing so. Our results suggest that the state of intergenerational relations in the United States is less dire than some might believe, and that high-quality contact with older adults is associated not only with less negative stereotypes but also younger people feeling both less troubled by and better able to cope with their own aging.

articles.title: “Creating a Culture that Fits Us Better”: Intersectional Stress and Relational Strengths in Non-heteronormative Intercultural Relationships
articles.authors: Elizabeth A. Georgopoulos, Micheal Weston
articles.abstract: This study examined the stressors experienced by individuals in non-heteronormative intercultural romantic relationships and investigated how they navigate these challenges to foster relationship satisfaction. Guided by a qualitative methodology rooted in interpretivist epistemology and constructionist ontology, we explored the lived experiences of 11 participants engaged in such relationships. Participants were recruited through purposive and snowball sampling. Semi-structured interviews were conducted to elicit participants’ reflections on relational dynamics, including cultural differences, minority stress, conflict, relational benefits, and resilience strategies within their unique social and cultural contexts. Through thematic analysis, we identified complex and intersectional stressors, such as systemic oppression, cultural value conflict, and identity invalidation, which were often exacerbated by environments lacking identity affirmation. Participants described employing protective strategies, including culturally attuned conflict negotiation, selective identity management, and engagement with identity-affirming communities. Despite these challenges, participants also reported relational strengths, such as the freedom to redefine inherited values and a deepened sense of authenticity. These findings highlight the importance of culturally responsive and identity-affirming support systems in psychological practice and relationship research. Such frameworks should account for the layered nature of minority stress while recognising the strengths and adaptive strategies individuals contribute to self-expansion, belonging, and love within non-heteronormative intercultural relationships.

articles.title: The Real-World Effects of Constructive Journalism: A Field Experiment on Climate Change News
articles.authors: Morten Skovsgaard
articles.abstract: To explore the effects of constructive journalism beyond one-shot experiments, this study utilizes a 2-week constructive journalism campaign on climate change in two regional Danish news outlets. Employing a difference-in-differences approach, news users exposed to the campaign were compared to news users from regions not exposed to the campaign. The constructive journalism campaign yielded more positive evaluations of news coverage, but not on core quality aspects like trustworthiness and balance. No effects were found for emotional responses, response efficacy, and behavioural intentions, but a positive effect was found for self-efficacy, indicating the potential of a constructive approach to journalism.

articles.title: Work-Related Harassment and Intimidation in Journalism: Testing Identity-, Visibility-, and Influence-Based Explanations
articles.authors: Ilmari Hiltunen, Ilari Törönen, Aleksi Suuronen, Reeta Pöyhtäri
articles.abstract: Prior research shows that exposure to occupation-related harassment and intimidation varies considerably across journalists. This study tests three explanatory frameworks for this variation: identity-based explanations attributing heightened exposure to social hierarchies; visibility- and celebrity-capital-based explanations linking it to journalists’ varying levels of personal visibility and recognizability; and influence-based explanations attributing differences to the nature of journalistic work and its societal influence. Logistic regression analyses of survey data from Finnish journalists ( n = 932), examining verbal, legal, and physical forms of harassment and intimidation, lend strong support to influence-based explanations, partial support to visibility-based explanations, and limited support to identity-based explanations.

articles.title: Toward Open Governance in Research Software for Communication and Media Research: Principles, Dimensions, and Practices
articles.authors: Florian Hohmann, Andreas Hepp, Karsten D. Wolf
articles.abstract: In recent years, communication and media studies have increasingly emphasized the need for open, transparent, and sustainable research infrastructures. Despite numerous calls for a cultural shift toward open science, the field continues to rely heavily on commercial and closed software environments that limit collaboration, reproducibility, and methodological innovation. This article responds to these challenges by examining two interconnected initiatives—MeTag/MeSort and OpenQDA—as examples of open, co-created research software developed at the University of Bremen. Building on the theoretical framing of research software as sociotechnical infrastructure, we introduce open governance as a conceptual framework for the sustainable management of research software. We argue that open governance is not merely a licensing issue but also a collaborative process of negotiating values, responsibilities, and practices among diverse stakeholders. Drawing insights from both case studies, we develop a conceptual model of open governance for research software that highlights the need for hybrid arrangements combining community-driven openness with structured coordination. In conclusion, we argue that such governance-oriented approaches represent a promising path toward sustainable, reusable, and equitable infrastructures for communication and media research.

articles.title: Building Deep Data Through Screens: Princeton-SMART for Mobile Communication Research
articles.authors: Jihye Lee, Kentaro Oriuchi, Daniel Muise, Jacob N. Shapiro
articles.abstract: This article introduces Princeton-SMART, open-source screen-capture software designed to generate deep data on mobile communication behavior. Princeton-SMART unobtrusively collects screenshots and on-screen text from Android devices at short intervals in naturalistic settings. We describe a research pipeline for secure data collection, preprocessing, and analysis, drawing on over 1.5 million screenshots contributed by U.S. job seekers over 6 weeks. We demonstrate how job-search activities can be identified using vision-language AI models and methodological considerations encountered during the process. We conclude by discussing opportunities and practical implications for integrating Princeton-SMART into mobile communication research.

articles.title: The Effects of Online Harassment of Scientists on Bystander Scientists
articles.authors: Jana Laura Egelhofer, Christina Seeger, Alice Binder
articles.abstract: Scientists who share research on social media increasingly face harassment, which is visible to many bystanders, including other scientists. We report a preregistered experiment testing how exposure to such harassment affects bystander scientists ( N = 846). Drawing on social identity approaches, we argue that bystander scientists may react similarly to directly targeted scientists. Results show that exposure to harassment increases anxiety and risk perceptions but does not reduce willingness to engage in science communication; it slightly increases perceived trustworthiness of targeted scientists. Presumed influence shapes some of these effects. Shifting attention to bystanders, we highlight broader societal consequences of harassment against scientists.

articles.title: When Movement Widens the Gap: The Contingent Effect of the Chinese #MeToo Movement on Feminist Attitudes
articles.authors: Shuning Lu, Haixin Mu, Tian Yang
articles.abstract: Social movements are often associated with various cultural outcomes, including shifts in public opinion regarding movement-related attitudes and ideologies. This study examines the shift of feminist attitudes among the public following the Chinese #MeToo movement. We develop a sociotechnical contingency framework that emphasizes how identity-based movement relevance and access to information channels shape the shifts in public opinion following social movements. Using nationally representative data from the Chinese General Social Survey (2010–2023), we find that the #MeToo movement was significantly associated with an increase in pro-feminist attitudes. These changes were unevenly distributed across groups, revealing widening attitudinal gaps along gender identities and digital divides. Our findings contribute to a nuanced understanding of how contemporary digitally mediated movements catalyze cultural change and underscore the need to contextualize their impact as it interacts with structural dynamics.

articles.title: ‘Seeing’ in the museums of South Asia: exploring visitors’ gaze
articles.authors: Akash Bharadwaj, Kumar Vivek
articles.abstract: Administrators and museum professionals in South Asia have often viewed visitors as passive, illiterate, or incapable of meaningful engagement, frequently characterising museums as 'Ajaib Ghars' (Houses of Wonder). Drawing on discussions such as Mark Elliott’s notion of 'side-effects' and Shaila Bhatti’s deployment of 'nazar'—an oblique, sensory, and culturally inflected mode of looking—this essay challenges such reductive perceptions by foregrounding vernacular and embedded practices of seeing in museums of South Asia. Further mobilising W. J. T. Mitchell’s conception of 'images as animate entities' and Karen Strassler’s idea of 'demanding images,' the essay proposes images as a method through which public perceptions of museums in South Asia can be both understood and critically examined. It does so by taking the Bihar Museum, one of the most ambitious museum projects of postcolonial India, as its site of analysis. Through this case, the essay develops five interpretive constructs—contemplation, intimacy, playfulness, remoteness, and indifference—which, while neither comprehensive nor fixed, together illuminate the dynamic and contested public character of the museum in the South Asian context.
